subject: Climate & Environment
title: Arrhenius and the First Warning
description: Learn Arrhenius and the First Warning in one minute.

hook.text: In 1896, a Swedish chemist calculated what doubling CO₂ would do to Earth's temperature.

buildup.text: Svante Arrhenius spent a year doing the math by hand — thousands of calculations.

discovery.text: He predicted about 5°C of warming. Modern estimates say 2.5 to 4.5°C. Close.

twist.text: Arrhenius thought warming would be good — longer growing seasons for Scandinavia.

climax.text: He was right about the physics but wrong about the outcome. The world ignored him.

punchline.text: The first climate prediction was done with pencil and paper.

quiz.question: What did Svante Arrhenius predict in 1896?

details.summary: In 1896, Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius calculated that doubling atmospheric CO2 would raise global temperatures by 5 to 6 degrees Celsius. He was the first scientist to quantify the link between fossil fuel emissions and warming, more than a century before modern climate models.
details.whyItMatters: Arrhenius's calculation shows that the science of climate change is not new. The physics has been understood for over a century; only action has been delayed.
takeaways: Arrhenius published his CO2-warming calculation in 1896
He estimated 5 to 6 degrees per CO2 doubling, close to modern upper estimates
He thought warming would take thousands of years at 1890s emission rates

faq.question: How accurate was Arrhenius's prediction?
faq.answer: His estimate of 5 to 6 degrees per CO2 doubling is on the high end but within the range of modern estimates of 2.5 to 4 degrees. He correctly identified the mechanism and the direction, though he underestimated how fast emissions would grow.

faq.question: Did Arrhenius consider warming a problem?
faq.answer: No. Living in cold Sweden, he viewed warming positively and predicted better crop yields at high latitudes. At 1890s emission rates, CO2 doubling seemed millennia away. No one anticipated the explosive growth of fossil fuel use in the 20th century.
